result: The ciliary photoreceptor (cPRC) circuit is hierarchically presynaptic to the rhabdomeric photoreceptor (rPRC) circuit in Platynereis larvae. Connectomics analysis revealed that cPRCs synapse on RGW interneurons, which in turn connect to the rPRC circuit at multiple levels including INsn premotor interneurons, INpreMN interneurons, and ventral motoneurons (vMNs). No reciprocal connections from rPRC to cPRC circuits were found.
evaluation: Claims C2, C19-C22, and C104-C106 are all supported by serial-section transmission electron microscopy connectomics data showing specific synaptic connections. The hierarchical organization is demonstrated by the presence of connections from cPRC to rPRC circuits but not vice versa. The anatomical reconstructions and connectivity matrices provide strong evidence for this circuit architecture.

result: Platynereis c-opsin1 is a UV-absorbing opsin with maximal absorption at 384 nm in the dark spectrum and 370 nm in the dark-light difference spectrum. This was demonstrated through in vitro reconstitution of purified c-opsin1 with 11-cis-retinal and absorption spectroscopy.
evaluation: Claims C3, C28, C29, C85, and C17 are supported by in vitro absorption spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2E. The experimental approach of expressing c-opsin1 in COS1 cells, reconstituting with 11-cis-retinal, and measuring absorption spectra is standard and appropriate. The UV absorption properties are clearly demonstrated.

result: Each ciliary photoreceptor cell (cPRC) in Platynereis has 12-15 basal bodies with extensively branched sensory cilia supported by single microtubule doublets. The total sensory membrane surface area is approximately 276 μm², about 10 times smaller than rat rod photoreceptors, suggesting sufficient sensitivity for acute light sensation.
evaluation: Claims C24-C27 and C112-C113 are supported by serial-section transmission electron microscopy data with detailed morphological measurements. The calculation of membrane surface area from measured ciliary dimensions is straightforward. The comparison to rat rods provides appropriate context, though the inference about sensitivity (C27) is reasonable but not directly tested.

result: Ciliary photoreceptors in Platynereis exhibit a high resting calcium level and respond to 405 nm light stimulation with transient hyperpolarization followed by depolarization. In contrast, 488 nm stimulation causes only prolonged hyperpolarization without subsequent depolarization. The depolarization occurs even when 405 nm light is switched off during the hyperpolarization phase.
evaluation: Claims C30-C34 and C86-C87 are supported by calcium imaging data using GCaMP6s shown in Figures 2F-H. The differential responses to 405 nm versus 488 nm light are clearly demonstrated. The observation that depolarization occurs after light offset (C34) is particularly interesting and well-documented. The interpretation of calcium changes as reflecting hyperpolarization/depolarization is standard.

result: UV stimulation of cPRCs activates specific postsynaptic neurons with wavelength-dependent responses. Four RGW interneurons follow cPRC activity patterns, two SNearly sensory neurons depolarize upon 405 nm stimulus onset, and two SNlate neurons depolarize during the rising phase of cPRC activity. RGW and SNearly neurons respond only to 405 nm but not 488 nm stimulation, while SNlate neurons show weaker responses to 488 nm.
evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 2I-J and supplementary figures. The identification of responding neurons is based on both position and connectivity data from the connectome. The wavelength-specific responses are clearly demonstrated through comparative experiments with 405 nm and 488 nm light.

result: Platynereis larvae exhibit UV-violet avoidance behavior characterized by downward swimming in response to non-directional UV light (340-420 nm) but not longer wavelengths. The action spectrum closely matches the c-opsin1 absorption spectrum, suggesting this behavior is mediated by non-pigmented ciliary photoreceptors.
evaluation: Claims C41-C44 and C49 are supported by behavioral assays in vertical column setups with monochromatic light shown in Figure 3A-B. The match between behavioral action spectrum and c-opsin1 absorption spectrum (C43) is a strong inference supported by the data. The use of non-directional light is appropriate to distinguish this from directional phototaxis.

result: UV avoidance behavior appears at 36 hours post fertilization (hpf) in Platynereis larvae, approximately coinciding with morphological differentiation of cPRCs (after 32 hpf), but long before adult eye differentiation (72 hpf). Phototaxis is already present at 27 hpf when larval eyespots are functional.
evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are supported by developmental behavioral assays shown in Figure 3C and citations to previous work on photoreceptor differentiation timing. The temporal correlation between cPRC morphological differentiation and UV avoidance onset (C47) is suggestive but not definitive proof of causation, though it is consistent with the overall model.

result: When stimulated with directional UV-violet light (340-400 nm) from above, Platynereis larvae initially swim upward (phototaxis) but then switch to downward swimming (UV avoidance). Blue/cyan light (440-600 nm) triggers only upward phototaxis. The swimming direction can be repeatedly switched by alternating wavelengths without habituation. This cannot be explained as wavelength-dependent alternation between positive and negative phototaxis since early-stage larvae are exclusively positively phototactic yet show the behavioral switch.
evaluation: Claims C50-C59 are supported by extensive behavioral assays with directional monochromatic light shown in Figures 3D-F and Video 2. The argument that this is not simply wavelength-dependent phototaxis switching (C59) is well-reasoned based on developmental data showing early larvae are only positively phototactic. The lack of habituation (C56) is demonstrated by repeated switching experiments.

result: Platynereis larvae respond to mixed wavelength light in a ratio-dependent manner. At high 380/480 nm ratios larvae swim downward, at low ratios upward, and at 40% ratio they remain at constant depth. Mixing UV with 660 nm red light (to which larvae don't respond phototactically) does not induce upward swimming at any ratio, demonstrating that UV intensity reduction alone doesn't cause the behavioral switch. These results are consistent with a ratio-chromatic depth gauge mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C60-C66 are supported by behavioral assays with mixed wavelength light shown in Figure 3G. The control experiment with 380/660 nm ratios (C63) is critical for ruling out simple intensity effects. The inference of a ratio-chromatic depth gauge (C66) is well-supported by the data combined with known properties of light attenuation in seawater, though direct ecological validation is not provided.

result: A c-opsin1 knockout line was generated by TALEN-mediated genome editing with an 8 bp deletion in exon 3. Homozygous c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 larvae have cPRCs with low resting calcium levels that neither hyperpolarize nor depolarize upon 405 nm stimulation, demonstrating that c-opsin1 is required for elevated resting calcium (indicating a dark current) and for light-induced responses.
evaluation: Claims C67-C72 are supported by genetic and calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4A-C. The TALEN approach is appropriate and the deletion is well-characterized. The loss of both resting calcium and light responses in mutants provides strong evidence for c-opsin1's role. The inference about dark current (C72) is reasonable based on comparison with vertebrate photoreceptors.

result: c-opsin1 knockout larvae show normal positive phototaxis to 480 nm blue light but have severely defective UV-avoidance responses. While wild-type larvae swim downward after initial upward swimming in UV light, c-opsin1Δ8/Δ8 mutants continue swimming upward, demonstrating that c-opsin1 is a critical mediator of UV-avoidance behavior.
evaluation: Claims C73-C75, C77, and C90 are supported by behavioral assays comparing wild-type and mutant larvae shown in Figure 4D. The preservation of blue-light phototaxis but loss of UV avoidance in mutants provides strong genetic evidence for c-opsin1's specific role in UV avoidance. The behavioral phenotype is clear and statistically significant.

result: The diminishing magnitude of upward swimming in c-opsin1 mutants under UV light (approaching zero displacement at 1.5-2 min) suggests an additional c-opsin1-independent UV-avoidance mechanism may exist. Loss of c-opsin1 is expected to disrupt the depth gauge since both cyan and UV light induce sustained positive phototaxis in mutants.
evaluation: Claim C76 is speculative based on incomplete loss of UV response in mutants. While the observation is valid, alternative explanations (e.g., incomplete penetrance, residual c-opsin1 function, or experimental variability) are not ruled out. Claim C78 is a logical inference but not directly tested. Additional experiments would be needed to confirm a second UV-sensing mechanism and to directly test depth gauge function in mutants.

result: A ratio-chromatic depth gauge in Platynereis larvae is formed by antagonistic interaction of two photoreceptor systems: rPRCs mediate phototaxis to UV-green wavelengths (380-540 nm) while cPRCs mediate UV-violet avoidance. Under UV-violet light, the avoidance response overrides phototaxis after ~30 seconds. At specific UV/blue ratios, the opposing behaviors cancel out. The UV-avoidance action spectrum matches c-opsin1 absorption spectrum.
evaluation: Claims C4, C79-C83, C88-C89 synthesize multiple lines of evidence including behavioral assays, spectroscopy, and knockout experiments. The antagonistic interaction is clearly demonstrated. The match between action and absorption spectra (C89) and the knockout phenotype provide strong support. The ~30 second timing (C82) is documented in behavioral data.

result: The ratio of blue/UV light increases with depth in seawater due to differential attenuation. Platynereis larvae may use this ratio as a depth gauge during vertical migration, allowing them to maintain a specific depth in the ocean.
evaluation: Claim C5 about light attenuation in seawater is well-established knowledge supported by citations. However, claims C6 and C84 about larvae actually using this as a depth gauge are speculative. While the behavioral data are consistent with this hypothesis, direct evidence of depth regulation in natural conditions is not provided. Field experiments or depth-dependent behavioral assays would be needed to confirm this ecological function.

result: The depolarizing response in cPRCs shows similar delayed onset as UV-violet avoidance behavior, suggesting the behavior is due to cPRC depolarization. Depolarization occurs even when stimulus light is switched off during hyperpolarization, implying it results from a sustained cell-autonomous or non-autonomous signal rather than direct opsin activation.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 are supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 2H showing depolarization after light offset. The temporal correlation between cPRC depolarization and behavior (C91) is reasonable but not rigorously quantified. The inference about sustained signaling (C93) is logical based on the light-off experiment, though the specific mechanism remains unknown.

result: The high calcium level in cPRCs suggests possible tonic neurotransmitter (likely acetylcholine) release in darkness, similar to vertebrate photoreceptors. Blue light (488 nm) induces cPRC hyperpolarization without subsequent depolarization, possibly mediated by another opsin such as c-opsin2 (λmax 490 nm). Hyperpolarization induced by violet versus blue light has different downstream consequences, potentially due to engagement of different signaling cascades.
evaluation: Claims C94-C99 are largely speculative. C94 is a reasonable inference by analogy to vertebrate photoreceptors but lacks direct evidence of neurotransmitter release. C95 is supported by calcium imaging data. C96-C97 about c-opsin2 are speculative suggestions without direct testing. C98 is supported by differential postsynaptic responses, but C99 about different signaling cascades is speculative without molecular evidence.

result: The cPRC circuit connects to Ser-h1 serotonergic ciliomotor neurons, suggesting ciliary activity modulation may contribute to UV avoidance. The cPRCs and their postsynaptic targets are part of the neurosecretory brain center, and knocking out one neuroendocrine signaling component causes strong UV avoidance defects. Cholinergic input from RGW cells to INsn premotor interneurons may antagonize phototaxis.
evaluation: Claims C100, C102 are supported by connectomics data and citations. However, C101 and C107 about functional roles are speculative inferences from connectivity. C103 mentions unpublished knockout data that would be important but cannot be evaluated. These claims suggest interesting mechanisms but require additional experimental validation.

result: Ciliary and rhabdomeric photoreceptor cells represent two main evolutionary lines in animals. Rhabdomeric PRCs have microvillar rhabdoms storing r-opsins and are found in most protostome eyes. Ciliary PRCs have specialized ciliary compartments storing c-opsins and form vertebrate rods and cones. Opsin class generally correlates with morphological type. Both cell types likely coexisted in the last common bilaterian ancestor.
evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C11 represent established knowledge in the field supported by extensive citations. These provide essential background context for the study. C11 about ancestral coexistence is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution, which is a standard evolutionary argument well-supported by comparative data.

result: In Platynereis, non-pigmented brain cPRCs with ramified cilia express c-opsin1. Pigmented larval eyespots and adult eyes mediate early- and late-stage phototaxis respectively. Trochophore larvae have eyespots with cholinergic r-opsin3-expressing rPRCs innervating the ciliary band. Nectochaete larvae develop adult eyes with rPRCs coexpressing multiple opsins. Previous work suggested cPRCs mediate circadian entrainment by UV light and could influence phototaxis.
evaluation: Claims C12-C16, C18, C23 are supported by citations to previous work on Platynereis photoreceptor systems. These provide essential background on the known functions of rPRCs and set up the question about cPRC function that this study addresses. C18 and C23 are inferences from prior work that motivated the current study.

result: The findings suggest ciliary and rhabdomeric photoreceptor types may have evolved antagonistic functions early in evolution. According to one hypothesis, as brain cPRCs were recruited for vision in vertebrates, rPRCs evolved into retinal ganglion cells, supported by melanopsin expression in intrinsically photosensitive ganglion cells. The vertebrate retina's cell-type mosaic may have originated from hierarchical integration of distinct cPRC and rPRC circuits mediating antagonistic behaviors.
evaluation: Claims C108-C111 are evolutionary hypotheses and speculations. C109-C110 cite existing hypotheses about photoreceptor evolution. C108 and C111 are new speculations based on the Platynereis findings. While these are interesting ideas consistent with the data, they are highly speculative and would require extensive comparative and evolutionary studies to test. The evidence from a single species is insufficient to draw broad evolutionary conclusions.

result: The four cholinergic cPRCs send axons to the neurosecretory plexus and synapse on RGW and NOS interneurons, as well as flask-shaped sensory-neurosecretory neurons expressing diverse neuropeptides but lacking postsynaptic partners. RGW cells synapse on Ser-h1 serotonergic cells that are part of the ciliomotor circuitry.
evaluation: Claims C114-C116 are supported by connectomics data and citations to previous work characterizing these cell types. These provide important anatomical details about the cPRC circuit organization and its connections to both neurosecretory and motor systems.
